concepts.label: Global Population Distribution
concepts.what: ~8 billion people distributed extremely unevenly — ~90% concentrated in ~30% of the land. Average of ~56 persons/sqkm if evenly spread; reality is dense clusters surrounded by vast near-empty zones (Sahara, Amazon, Tibetan Plateau, Arctic). Distribution follows substrate liveability.

concepts.label: Three Major Population Clusters
concepts.what: South Asia (Indo-Gangetic plain and Bay of Bengal deltas — densest), East Asia (China's eastern plains, Japan's narrow coastal strips — largest by number), Western Europe (thinner and more evenly spread, product of industrialisation). Smaller dense pockets: Northeast USA, Nile valley, parts of Southeast Asia.

concepts.label: Factors Determining Population Distribution
concepts.what: Physical — flat fertile terrain at low altitude preferred; mountains and high plateaus avoided; water availability (river valleys and coastlines attract settlement); temperate and monsoonal climates more supportive; fertile soils. Economic — mineral concentration attracts industry (Chotanagpur plateau); transport corridors thicken population. Social-political — stable governance, religious centres, kinship networks sustain density; conflict evacuates.

concepts.label: Demographic Transition Theory
concepts.what: Five-stage sequence: Stage 1 — high birth and death rates, stable low population (pre-industrial agrarian). Stage 2 — death rate falls while birth rate stays high, producing explosive growth (sub-Saharan Africa in late 20th century). Stage 3 — birth rate begins falling (female education, lower child mortality, higher urban costs), growth slows (most of Asia in last two generations). Stage 4 — both rates low and stable, population flat (Europe, Japan). Stage 5 — births below replacement (~2.1/woman), population shrinking (Japan, Germany, South Korea, parts of Southern Europe).

concepts.label: India's Demographic Divide — 1921
concepts.what: 1921 is the official demographic divide — before it, population was essentially stagnant; after it, steady growth began. Four phases: stagnant (pre-1921), steady (1921–1951), explosive (1951–1981, driven by vaccines, Green Revolution, famine prevention), declining growth rate (1981 onwards). India now in late Stage 3 pressing against Stage 4; growth rate fell from above 2% annually in the 1970s to ~1% now.

concepts.label: Demographic Dividend
concepts.what: The window during which the working-age share of the population peaks relative to the young and old — a temporary economic opportunity if schools, skills, and jobs follow the demography. India's demographic dividend is currently open and estimated to remain open until roughly 2055. The demography alone guarantees nothing; conversion into actual development requires deliberate policy.

concepts.label: India's Population Size and Density
concepts.what: ~1.41 billion as of 2023 — recently overtook China as world's most populous country. 17.5% of world's population on 2.4% of its land area. National average density 382 persons/sqkm in 2011 census; current estimates ~470.

concepts.label: State-level Density Variations
concepts.what: Extreme range. Dense end: Bihar (1,106/sqkm), West Bengal (1,028), Kerala (860), Uttar Pradesh (829). Sparse end: Arunachal Pradesh (17), Mizoram (52), Sikkim (86). Physical substrate explanation: alluvial plains of Ganga and tributaries support dense settled agriculture; forested hill states of the northeast do not.

concepts.label: India's Age Structure
concepts.what: ~29% under 14, ~64% in the working-age band (15–64), ~7% above 65; median age ~28 years. Relatively young structure — the demographic dividend in numerical form. Workable window remains open for several decades.

concepts.label: Sex Ratio in India — Spatial Pattern
concepts.what: 940 females per 1,000 males in 2011 — below world average. Spatial pattern reveals social geography. South and east markedly better: Kerala (1,084), Tamil Nadu (996), Andhra Pradesh (993). Northwest prosperous agricultural belt markedly worse: Haryana (879), Punjab (895), Delhi (868). Northwest's agrarian prosperity coexists with a patriarchal inheritance that has historically treated daughters as liabilities. The south's higher ratios reflect Dravidian cultural tradition with stronger female autonomy and, in Kerala's case, a century of investment in female literacy.

concepts.label: PCPNDT Act 1994
concepts.what: Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act. Prohibits sex-selective abortion and the use of diagnostic techniques (ultrasound) for sex determination before or after conception. Enacted as a legislative response to the documented sex ratio deficit in the prosperous northwest agricultural belt — a case of law following demography.

concepts.label: Literacy Rate in India
concepts.what: National literacy rate 74% in 2011; males 82%, females 65.5%. Kerala 93.9% (highest). Bihar 63.8% (lowest major state). Female literacy is a direct predictor of sex ratio, fertility rate, and child health outcomes — its geographic distribution mirrors and explains several other social indicators.

concepts.label: Religious Composition of India (Census 2011)
concepts.what: Hindu 79.8%, Muslim 14.2%, Christian 2.3%, Sikh 1.7%, Buddhist 0.7%, Jain 0.4%. From the 2011 census. Largest Muslim-majority concentrations in Jammu & Kashmir, Assam, West Bengal (border districts), Kerala, and the UP-Bihar belt.

concepts.label: Rural-Urban Split
concepts.what: 31% urban in 2011; currently estimated at ~36%. India remains a majority-rural country despite its GDP level — unusual for an economy at comparable income, most of which were already above 50% urban. A structural feature of India's development path: service and IT sectors grew without urbanising the population at equivalent pace.

concepts.label: Human Development Index (HDI)
concepts.what: Introduced in 1990 by Mahbub ul-Haq in collaboration with Amartya Sen's capability framework. Combines life expectancy, education, and per capita income adjusted for purchasing power into a single number between 0 and 1. India sits in the medium-development tier, around 134th out of 193 countries in recent rankings — well below where its economic size alone would place it. The gap between GDP rank and HDI rank is a political fact: how growth has been distributed and what it has, so far, failed to reach.

concepts.label: Four Types of Migration Streams
concepts.what: Rural-to-rural (largest by volume, dominated by women moving on marriage across district boundaries), rural-to-urban (dominated by men seeking employment), urban-to-urban, and urban-to-rural. India in 2001: ~307 million people (30% of population) living somewhere other than where they were born — migration is a structural feature of the country's geography, not an exception.

concepts.label: Push-Pull Framework of Migration
concepts.what: Push factors make origin places intolerable: poverty, landlessness, flood, drought, slow wages. Pull factors make destinations attractive: jobs, schools, hospitals, anonymity and reinvention. The framework organises cause without determining direction — specific corridors are shaped by the industrial geography of receiving states.

concepts.label: Inter-State Migration Corridors
concepts.what: UP and Bihar are dominant net out-migration states (UP net −2.6 million, Bihar net −1.7 million in early 2000s). Maharashtra, Delhi, Gujarat, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu are dominant net in-migration destinations (Maharashtra net +2.3 million; greater Mumbai highest absolute urban in-migration of any city). The flow: poor east to industrialising west and south, feeding construction, textiles, and domestic-service economies of receiving states.

concepts.label: Seasonal/Circular Migration
concepts.what: Agricultural labourers from Bihar, Odisha, Rajasthan, and Madhya Pradesh move for 4–8 months for harvest or construction then return — never counted as migrants in any census. Structurally invisible in normal data. The 2020 COVID lockdown suddenly made this population visible: millions stranded mid-transit, walking hundreds of kilometres home, became a national emergency.

concepts.label: India's External Diaspora and Remittances
concepts.what: ~32 million people across 110+ countries — one of the world's largest diasporas. India receives the world's largest remittance flow, ~$125 billion annually. Remittances exceed FDI inflows in most years and are more stable as a financing source.

concepts.label: Three Waves of Indian Diaspora
concepts.what: First wave (colonial period) — involuntary indentured labour system sent millions from UP and Bihar to Mauritius, Trinidad, Tobago, Guyana, Fiji, South Africa as plantation workers. Second wave (1970s onwards) — Gulf oil boom drew unskilled workers from Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh to UAE, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, Kuwait; transferred remittances, not skills. Third wave (1960s onwards) — skilled professionals and students moving to USA, UK, Canada, Australia, Singapore, Malaysia.

concepts.label: Forced Migration Streams
concepts.what: Tibetan refugees (post-1959), Sri Lankan Tamil refugees (post-1983), Bangladeshi migration (post-1971, ongoing), Rohingya refugees (post-2017). A separate and politically fraught category from voluntary migration: these flows were produced by state violence and persecution rather than economic opportunity. Each stream has distinct legal and political status in India.

concepts.label: Clustered (Compact) Rural Settlement
concepts.what: Houses tightly packed, fields outside — dominant in the fertile alluvial plains of the Indo-Gangetic plain and the northeast. Abundance of water and flat farmland makes dense clustering rational; historical needs of defence and irrigation management reinforced it. The most common settlement form in India's most populous regions.

concepts.label: Semi-Clustered Rural Settlement
concepts.what: Dominant castes' main village surrounded by smaller hamlets of other communities — partial dispersal reflecting social fracture rather than physical necessity. Appears in Punjab, Haryana, and parts of Rajasthan. Settlement form encodes caste geography at a visible spatial scale.

concepts.label: Hamleted Rural Settlement
concepts.what: A single named village on the map is actually several discrete sub-villages — called panna, para, palli, nagla, or dhani in different regional dialects — separated physically but grouped administratively. Common in the lower Ganga plain, West Bengal, and Chhattisgarh. Reflects ethnic and caste separation at a fine spatial grain.

concepts.label: Dispersed Rural Settlement
concepts.what: Isolated farmsteads or huts separated by fields and forest — appears where terrain makes clustering impossible or social organisation does not require it: Himalayan slopes, Meghalaya, Uttarakhand, and Kerala's hilly laterite interior. Farming individual plots on steep terrain makes proximity to other households less valuable.

concepts.label: India's Census Definition of Urban Areas
concepts.what: Triple census criterion: (1) minimum population of 5,000; (2) population density at least 400/sqkm; (3) at least 75% of male working population in non-agricultural activities. Plus all statutory towns — declared under a state municipal act regardless of size or density. The third criterion (75% non-agri) distinguishes a genuine town from a large agricultural village and struggles most with India's semi-urbanised fringes.

concepts.label: Statutory Towns vs Census Towns
concepts.what: Statutory towns are declared under a state municipal act and count as urban regardless of satisfying census criteria. Census towns are settlements meeting the three demographic and occupational criteria but without formal municipal status — a large and growing category as India's semi-urban fringe expands.

concepts.label: Census Town Classification (Class I–VI)
concepts.what: Six classes by population: Class I (above 100,000 — roughly 500 in India), Class II (50,000–100,000), Class III (20,000–50,000), Class IV (10,000–20,000), Class V (5,000–10,000), Class VI (below 5,000). Cities above 1 million (~50) are metropolitan; those above 10 million are megacities.

concepts.label: Indian Megacities and Metropolitan Areas
concepts.what: Megacities (above 10 million): Delhi NCR, Mumbai MMR, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad — in roughly that order. Most large cities are multifunctional, though each retains functional origins that shaped urban morphology. Mumbai simultaneously commercial, industrial, educational, and administrative.

concepts.label: Functional Classification of Urban Centres
concepts.what: Administrative (Delhi, Bhubaneswar, Gandhinagar), Industrial (Jamshedpur, Bhilai), Transport and Port (Vishakhapatnam, Mughalsarai, Itarsi), Commercial (Mumbai, Kolkata), Mining (Dhanbad, Singrauli), Religious (Varanasi, Tirupati, Madurai, Amritsar, Ajmer), Educational (Pilani, Roorkee), Tourist (Shimla, Goa). Most large cities eventually become multifunctional; functional origin shapes urban morphology long after it ceases to dominate.

concepts.label: Conurbation (Patrick Geddes, 1915)
concepts.what: Term coined by Patrick Geddes in 1915 for the merging of adjacent urban areas into a functionally connected urban region. The precursor concept to megalopolis; describes urban expansion that erases physical gaps between previously separate towns and cities. Standard tool in urban geography since early 20th century.

concepts.label: Megalopolis (Jean Gottmann, 1957)
concepts.what: Coined by Jean Gottmann in 1957. Archetypal case: Boswash corridor (Northeast USA — Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, Washington) — near-continuous urbanised zone of ~50 million people. Pacific counterpart: Tokaido megalopolis in Japan (Tokyo to Osaka via Nagoya and Kyoto). A twentieth-century invention as automobile infrastructure and industrial expansion dissolved rural buffers between cities.

concepts.label: India's Emerging Urban Corridors
concepts.what: India's corridors still forming. Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC) and Chennai-Bengaluru Industrial Corridor are the two most actively planned and promoted. Unlike Boswash or Tokaido (which emerged organically from industrial geography), India's corridors are state-planned — industrial investment zones designed to accelerate the merger of urban regions along national highway and freight rail spines.
